name: 2 Kings

facts.author: The author is not known. Jewish tradition holds that Jeremiah the prophet wrote 1 and 2 Kings, which were once one book, using the court records of the kings.
facts.audience: The people of Israel in exile in Babylon, to show why the kingdom fell and to call them back to God

about: 2 Kings continues the story of the two kingdoms. Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2:11), and Elisha carries on his work. Elisha does many miracles: he raises the Shunammite woman's son, and God heals Naaman the Syrian of leprosy when he washes in the Jordan.

Most kings of Israel do evil, and God sends prophet after prophet to warn them (17:13). In the end the Assyrians take Samaria and carry the northern tribes into exile (17:6). Judah lasts longer. Good kings such as Hezekiah, who trusts the Lord when Assyria attacks (18:5), and Josiah, who finds the book of the law and turns to the Lord with all his heart (23:25), bring times of reform. But wicked kings such as Manasseh lead the people far from God.

At last Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon destroys Jerusalem and burns the temple, and the people are taken away. Yet the book ends with a small sign of hope: King Jehoiachin is set free from prison in Babylon (25:27).

themes.title: Judgement for sin
themes.text: Both kingdoms are sent into exile because they forsook the Lord and would not listen to His prophets.

themes.title: The power of God's word
themes.text: Through Elijah and Elisha God shows that He is the living God, and every word of His prophets comes true.

themes.title: Trust and reform
themes.text: Kings who trust the Lord and keep His law, like Hezekiah and Josiah, see God's help.

themes.title: Hope for David's line
themes.text: Even in exile, God keeps David's family alive, as He had promised.
